title: Imbalanced People: why a great hire is infinitely better than average ones
summary: Jason Cohen argues the "10x developer" idea understates reality: a great person in any role (developer, designer, writer, manager, support, product, sales) produces ideas and results that 100 average people never will. Because of this, he says you can't afford to hire anyone less than great.

principles.text: A great performer is not 10x an average one; they are better than any number of average people, because they create ideas others wouldn't.
principles.quote: A great developer, or a great designer, is more than 10x an average one--they're better than an infinite number.  Because they'll come up with ideas and implementations that 100 others wouldn't.

principles.text: The greatness rule holds in every role, including sales, support, management and product.
principles.quote: In fact, if you think there's any position at your company where this rule of "better than 10x" doesn't hold, you've never worked with greatness at that position.

principles.text: A great salesperson creates thrilled, referenceable customers and rallies the whole company around growth, rather than just closing leads.
principles.quote: A great salesperson is a factory producing cheerleader customers who are actually thrilled and referenceable after the sale

principles.text: Great managers develop their people's careers; average managers are just glorified project managers.
principles.quote: A great manager who develops the careers of their folks versus several average ones who are glorified project managers.

principles.text: Since greatness is a universal rule, you can't afford to hire less; if rivals can hire the best and you don't, you need a special plan to still win.
principles.quote: Now, if you understand this universal, timeless, human rule, you then realize you cannot afford to hire anyone less.

principles.text: Work with the best: you do amazing things together and learn daily, and life is too short for mediocrity.
principles.quote: Life's too short, and high tech moves too fast, to mess about with mediocrity.
